qs.q: The 'screw-home' mechanism of the knee joint involves passive medial rotation of the femur on the tibia during terminal extension. This mechanism causes tightening of which primary ligament, contributing to knee stability?
qs.e: The screw-home mechanism tightens both the collateral and cruciate ligaments, but the tibial (medial) collateral ligament is particularly important in resisting external rotation and providing stability in full extension, along with the anterior cruciate ligament. The question asks for a primary ligament that becomes tight due to the mechanism, and the MCL is a strong contributor to full extension stability.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - May 22, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The femur is the longest bone, forming the thigh and supporting weight. Its anatomy dictates joint mechanics, blood flow, and common injury patterns. Clinicians use this knowledge to diagnose fractures, assess vascular status, and plan surgeries.

sections.p: The femur is the largest and strongest bone, extending from the hip to the knee. It bears most of the body’s weight and provides attachment for major muscle groups.
It consists of a proximal head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, shaft, and distal condyles. The head articulates with the acetabulum, while the condyles meet the tibia.
Anteriorly lies the quadriceps tendon and patella; posteriorly the hamstrings. Medially and laterally, the femur is adjacent to the iliac crest and tibia.
The femoral artery gives off the profunda femoris and perforating branches. The nutrient artery enters the shaft, while the epiphyseal arteries supply the head and neck.

t.b: Details complex fractures and bone loss
Assesses soft tissue and vascular injury

sections.p: The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh; the obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh; the sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh.
The femur allows hip flexion, extension, abduction, and rotation, and knee flexion and extension. It transfers weight from the pelvis to the lower limb.
Fractures of the neck, shaft, and distal femur are common. Avascular necrosis follows neck fractures. Osteolytic lesions may indicate metastases.
On exam, assess femoral pulse, capillary refill, and distal neurovascular status. A positive Trendelenburg sign suggests hip abductor weakness.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with deformity, inability to bear weight, loss of distal pulses, or neuro deficits

faq.q: What causes avascular necrosis after a femoral neck fracture?
faq.a: Disruption of the medial circumflex femoral artery leads to bone death.

faq.q: How does a distal femur fracture present?
faq.a: Pain, swelling, and inability to extend the knee; the leg may be shortened.

faq.q: Why is the femur prone to osteolytic metastases?
faq.a: It has rich red marrow and venous plexus that allow tumor spread.
